parts.problem_md:
Ali rolls a fair six-sided dice labelled 1 to 6.

Ali gets a point when the dice lands on a number greater than 4.

Let $M$ denote the event that Ali's dice lands on a number greater than 4 when rolled.

He rolls the dice twice.

Complete the tree diagram.

![Probability tree diagram with two main branches labelled "M" and "M'" with fractions 2/3 and 2/6 leading to outcomes "M" and "M'".](assets/005-probability-tree-diagram-with-two-main-branches-.png)
parts.solution_md:
> *The events are independent, rolling the dice once does not change the probability of the next*

> $M$*  and *$M'$* are mutually exclusive and exhaustive events meaning that the sum of their probabilities must be 1*

> **[exam-tip]**
> In other words, the branches at a given split must add to 1 and therefore
> 
> $\mathrm{P} ( M ) + \frac{2}{3} = 1
> \mathrm{P} ( M ) = 1 - \frac{2}{3} 
> \mathrm{P} ( M ) = 1 \frac{1}{3}$
> 
> You can also find this by counting the number of possibilities. The number can land on six numbers, two of which are greater than 4.
> 
> $\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}$

![Probability tree diagram with branches showing fractions 2/6 and 2/3, leading to nodes labelled M and M' at each split.](assets/006-probability-tree-diagram-with-branches-showing-f.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> 
> **B1:** Fully correct tree diagram.

parts.problem_md: Calculate the probability that he lands on 4 or less at least once.
parts.solution_md:
> *The paths where at least one *$M'$* occurs are:*

$MM'\,M'M\,M'M'$

**[M1]**

> *Multiplying along the paths*

$M\timesM'=\frac{2}{9}\,M'\timesM=\frac{2}{9}\,M'\timesM'=\frac{4}{9}$

> *Adding all these paths together*

$\frac{2}{9}+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{4}{9}=\frac{8}{9}$

$\frac{8}{9}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You can also simply subtract the event of on $M'$ occurring, which is the same as the event that two $M$ occur. Since you worked this out in part b, $1-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{8}{9}$
